summary: planetXplorer is a web tool for exploring how the sky changes over time using SPHEREx data. Users enter the Coordinates, FOV. Alligned images in a timeline is then displayed. The app retrieves IRSA and uses our algorithms to process data. Archive searches, image processing, and visual comparision controls are brought into one singular interface, helping people examine public astronomy data with ease. PlanetXplorer supports the visual investigation of possible changes, and is made to be modular so it could accept new values when released by NASA.
details:
Planet X is a browser-based app for inspecting changes in NASA SPHEREx images over time. It addresses the practical work between finding archive records and viewing a useful sequence, providing ui for: selecting observation dates, retrieving scientific images, aligning the same sky region, and preserving the context needed to interpret what appears on screen.

Users enter right ascension and declination, choose an angular field of view, and optionally set dates and observation spacing. The backend queries Caltech/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), discovers spectral images from DR1 and QR3, reorganizes data for displaying in a time sequence, and downloads selected FITS cutouts. The full catalog remains available, and the default 60-day spacing creates separated dates from one detector. Users can reveal closely spaced exposures when shorter time intervals are useful.

The backend reads image, quality, variance, and coordinate information. It masks invalid pixels and aligns usable images to a common sky grid. The frontend displays those scientific pixels with playback, frame stepping, timeline scrubbing, zoom, pan, and inversion. It can also create custom color assignments for each spectrum. Checkboxes determine which loaded observations are used, and a Load checked action retrieves selected records that are not yet available. Acquisition-date gaps are displayed independently of the screen playback delay.

Scientific interpretation and accuracy is part of the design. Browse mode supports chronological inspection, while Matched mode restricts playback to compatible wavelength and calibration groups when available. Observation identifiers, dates, detector information, archive links, and failure reasons remain accessible. Additional details such as pixel flags, spectral intensity graphs are also provided for the more technical.
The workflow is taken into account. Shared URLs restore the searched field, and a CSV export supports follow-up inspection of the catalog. The import/export saved locations feature is also useful for sharing discoveries in an organized, catalogued manner.

One additional feature is the use of Aladin to show positions of known objects directly on the display. By clicking on them, further information is also revealed

The front end uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and HTML Canvas for the interface. The backend uses FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, Reproject, and Pillow for data retrieval and image preparation as the resources recommended python. The frontend and backend are hosted separately on Vercel and Render. The prototype uses a disposable cache in the front end in place of a back end database.

The intended benefit is to let students, astronomy enthusiasts, and citizen scientists examine public observations through a single interface instead of building their own archive-processing workflow. Backend and browser automation cover processing and interaction.
Real archive checks include a Barnard's Star field with two loaded images separated by approximately 192 days. That verifies retrieval and date separation; it is not a verified motion detection. Full motion and variability validation across all five challenge targets remains in progress. Further astronomical checks are needed.
